demo-wpss-project.title: Workplace Psychological Safety Scale (WPSS)
demo-wpss-project.description: Development and psychometric validation of a 12-item multidimensional measure of workplace psychological safety for contemporary cross-functional work teams.
demo-wpss-project.targetPopulation: Employed adults working in team-based knowledge and service settings
demo-wpss-project.intendedInterpretation: Diagnostic and empirical assessment of team psychological safety climate to inform organizational development and research modeling.
demo-wpss-project.measurementModelJustification: Psychological safety is conceptualized as an unobserved shared climate trait causing observable indicators (comfortable speaking up, error admission, mutual support). If safety increases, all indicators are expected to shift positively.

existingInstrumentsReviewed.name: Edmondson (1999) 7-Item Team Psychological Safety Scale
existingInstrumentsReviewed.citation: Edmondson, A. (1999). Psychological safety and learning behavior in work teams. Administrative Science Quarterly, 44(2), 350-383.
existingInstrumentsReviewed.whyInsufficient: Predominantly unidimensional and concise (7 items); incorporates 3 reverse-coded items that frequently produce method-effect artifacts in EFA; does not differentiate between voice safety, error tolerance, and peer support dimensions required for granular workplace intervention diagnostics.

existingInstrumentsReviewed.name: Clark (2020) 4 Stages of Psychological Safety Framework
existingInstrumentsReviewed.citation: Clark, T. R. (2020). The 4 Stages of Psychological Safety: Defining the Path to Inclusion and Innovation. Berrett-Koehler Publishers.
existingInstrumentsReviewed.whyInsufficient: Widely used in executive coaching but originally conceptualized as a practitioner model; lacks peer-reviewed cross-cultural CFA invariance validation and published item parameters in open science repositories.

existingInstrumentsReviewed.name: Liang, Farh & Farh (2012) Psychological Safety for Voice Scale
existingInstrumentsReviewed.citation: Liang, J., Farh, C. I., & Farh, J. L. (2012). Psychological antecedents of promotive and prohibitive voice. Academy of Management Journal, 55(1), 71-92.
existingInstrumentsReviewed.whyInsufficient: Concentrates specifically on oral speaking-up and vocal dissent; omits collaborative error reporting, asking for help, and behavioral experimentation facets.

existingInstrumentsReviewed.name: Brown & Leigh (1996) Psychological Safety Climate Scale
existingInstrumentsReviewed.citation: Brown, S. P., & Leigh, T. W. (1996). A new look at psychological climate. Journal of Applied Psychology, 81(4), 358-368.
existingInstrumentsReviewed.whyInsufficient: Focuses heavily on management/supervisory flexibility and supportive management style rather than lateral peer-to-peer psychological vulnerability among team colleagues.

existingInstrumentsReviewed.name: Carmeli & Gittell (2009) Relational Psychological Safety Scale
existingInstrumentsReviewed.citation: Carmeli, A., & Gittell, J. H. (2009). High-quality relationships, psychological safety, and learning from failures. Journal of Organizational Behavior, 30(6), 709-729.
existingInstrumentsReviewed.whyInsufficient: Assumes co-located relational coordination and does not capture dissent safety or psychological safety in contemporary asynchronous digital team communication.

existingInstrumentsReviewed.name: O'Donovan & McAuliffe (2020) Healthcare Team Safety Scale
existingInstrumentsReviewed.citation: O'Donovan, R., & McAuliffe, E. (2020). Exploring psychological safety in healthcare teams to inform the development of an intervention: a qualitative and psychometric study. BMJ Open, 10(7), e038392.
existingInstrumentsReviewed.whyInsufficient: Domain-specific clinical wording (consultants, patient incidents, clinical procedures) limits generalizability to non-healthcare knowledge worker settings.

constructDefinition.conceptualDefinition: A shared psychological belief held by members of a work team that the team environment is safe for interpersonal risk-taking, characterized by confidence that one will not be humiliated, rejected, or blamed for speaking up with ideas, questions, concerns, or mistakes.
constructDefinition.theoreticalFramework: Social Information Processing Theory (Salancik & Pfeffer, 1978) combined with Edmondson’s (1999) Team Psychological Safety Framework.

supportingLiterature.citation: Churchill, G. A. (1979). A paradigm for developing better measures of marketing constructs. JMR.
supportingLiterature.keyProposition: Requires conceptual boundary delimitation, rigorous domain sampling, and item purification.

supportingLiterature.citation: Clark, L. A., & Watson, D. (2019). Constructing validity: New developments in creating objective measuring instruments. Assessment.
supportingLiterature.keyProposition: Stresses distinct factor identification and testing on independent cross-validation samples.

supportingLiterature.citation: Boateng, G. O., et al. (2018). Best practices for developing and validating scales. Frontiers in Public Health.
supportingLiterature.keyProposition: Systematizes the 9-phase scale development roadmap from item pool to invariance.

includedAspects: Willingness and perceived freedom to voice constructive critique
Tolerance and constructive learning orientation toward errors
Perceived interpersonal acceptance and reciprocal peer assistance
excludedAspects: Satisfaction with physical workplace environment or compensation
Toleration of malicious negligence or intentional policy violations

relatedConstructsDiscriminant.distinctionRationale: Trust is expectation of benign behavior by others; psychological safety is the climate in which one feels safe to act vulnerably.
Deliberate individual self-presentation versus shared collective social climate.
Silence is behavioral withholding; safety is the cognitive/affective perception that makes silence unnecessary.

dimensions.name: Voice & Dissent Safety
dimensions.description: The shared belief that expressing candid disagreement, asking challenging questions, and raising constructive critique will not lead to personal penalties or humiliation.
dimensions.includedAspects: Speaking up about team workflow issues, questioning prevailing group consensus, voicing dissenting views.
dimensions.excludedAspects: General extroversion, interpersonal chattiness, aggressive confrontation.

dimensions.name: Error Tolerance & Learning
dimensions.description: The perception that well-intentioned mistakes and procedural slip-ups are treated as learning opportunities rather than occasions for blame, scapegoating, or punitive action.
dimensions.includedAspects: Acknowledging honest errors openly, learning collectively from project missteps, absence of scapegoating.
dimensions.excludedAspects: Gross negligence, tolerating intentional misconduct or violation of safety rules.

dimensions.name: Mutual Support & Inclusion
dimensions.description: The belief that team members value one another’s unique competencies, offer mutual assistance during difficulties, and avoid undermining or rejecting colleagues.
dimensions.includedAspects: Valuing diverse perspectives, reciprocal help-seeking, feeling accepted as a whole person.
dimensions.excludedAspects: Superficial friendliness, social popularity, off-work social cohesion.

items.wording: I feel comfortable raising difficult issues and questions during team meetings.
items.sourceOrRationale: Deductive derivation from Edmondson (1999) voice safety definition and qualitative pilot themes.

revisions.previousWording: I can speak up about problems without fear.
revisions.newWording: I feel comfortable raising difficult issues and questions during team meetings.
revisions.rationale: Specified behavioral context (team meetings) following cognitive interview feedback indicating ambiguity.
revisions.author: Lead Researcher

items.wording: In this team, it is acceptable to express disagreement with established opinions.
items.sourceOrRationale: Clark & Watson (2019) domain sampling for dissent tolerance.

items.wording: I can challenge popular ideas on this team without worrying about being marginalized.
items.sourceOrRationale: Synthesized from focus group interviews with cross-functional project teams.

items.wording: Team members actively encourage colleagues to share unconventional perspectives.
When someone on this team makes an honest mistake, it is treated as a learning opportunity.
items.sourceOrRationale: Adapted from organizational learning climate literature (Edmondson, 1999).

items.wording: Mistakes made during work are frequently held against you by team members.
items.sourceOrRationale: Reverse-scored indicator capturing punitive blame culture.
items.reverseRationale: Captures direct interpersonal threat and retaliatory blame; scored reversely so high scores reflect safety.

items.wording: Team members freely admit their procedural errors without fearing ridicule.
items.sourceOrRationale: Grounded in psychological safety error transparency dimensions.

items.wording: Our team focuses on resolving issues rather than assigning personal blame.
items.sourceOrRationale: Hinkin (1998) guideline for clear behavioral referents.

items.wording: My team members value and utilize the unique skills that each person brings.
items.sourceOrRationale: Construct coverage for perceived team member valuation.

items.wording: It is easy to ask colleagues on this team for help when encountering a roadblock.
Members of this team genuinely support one another during high-pressure periods.
People in this team sometimes reject colleagues who think or act differently.
items.reverseRationale: Captures social rejection; inverted during scoring so high values indicate high mutual inclusion.

items.wording: I feel comfortable asking questions and requesting promotions from team leadership.
items.sourceOrRationale: Initial candidate item generated during brainstorming.
items.statusRationale: Removed following expert review and cognitive testing: double-barrelled prompt conflating routine questions with career advancement requests (I-CVI = 0.50).

heuristicFlags.message: Item combines two distinct inquiries ("asking questions" vs "requesting promotions").
heuristicFlags.suggestion: Separate into distinct questions or eliminate career advancement inquiry.

items.wording: No one on this team ever makes mistakes or experiences project failure.
items.sourceOrRationale: Initial candidate item tested for negative contrast.
items.statusRationale: Removed due to extreme absolute wording ("never") causing ceiling/floor distortion and theoretical mismatch with psychological safety concept.

heuristicFlags.message: Absolute qualifier "never" distorts variance and reduces item discrimination.

expertPanels.name: Content Validity Panel (Psychometrics & Org Psych)
expertPanels.description: Expert evaluation of item relevance, linguistic clarity, and construct coverage in organizational teams.

ratings.qualitativeComments: Conflates psychological safety with formal promotional negotiations.

overallComments.comment: Strong theoretical alignment with Edmondson’s foundational conceptualization. The 3 proposed dimensions cover the core operational facets cleanly.
Recommend deleting WPSS-13 as it violates psychometric single-idea rules. All other 12 items demonstrate high content clarity.

cognitiveInterviews.paraphrasedMeaning: Understood as feeling secure when questioning the team sprint priorities or calling out code architecture flaws.
cognitiveInterviews.retrievalStrategy: Recalled specific team retrospectives from last month.

cognitiveInterviews.paraphrasedMeaning: Understood as whether reporting a near-miss or medication logging delay leads to informal punishment or disciplinary threats.
cognitiveInterviews.retrievalStrategy: Reflected on unit incident reporting policies.
cognitiveInterviews.responseMappingDifficulty: Noted that this item is reversed compared to others, but easily comprehensible.

cognitiveInterviews.paraphrasedMeaning: Confused between asking advice on lesson plans versus demanding salary increases from the principal.
cognitiveInterviews.retrievalStrategy: Expressed hesitation: "Those are two completely different things in our school."
cognitiveInterviews.responseMappingDifficulty: Could not choose a single rating.

validationHypotheses.rationale: Edmondson (1999) theoretical model establishes psychological safety as the primary psychological antecedent enabling teams to engage in collective experimentation, error analysis, and feedback-seeking.

empiricalResult.interpretation: Strong positive correlation supporting convergent construct validity (r = .58, p < .001).

validationHypotheses.rationale: Psychological safety is a climate-level shared belief, not an individual self-enhancement or response bias trait. Correlation with social desirability scales should be negligible.

empiricalResult.interpretation: Weak, non-consequential correlation (|r| = .16 <= .30) supporting discriminant divergence from response bias.

validationHypotheses.rationale: Higher climate safety should substantially reduce intentional withholding of critical ideas, feedback, or error disclosures (Detert & Edmondson, 2011).

empiricalResult.interpretation: Significant negative concurrent criterion correlation (r = -.54, p < .001) as hypothesized.

decisionLog.title: New Instrument Development Justification over Existing Scales
decisionLog.rationalSummary: Existing scales (e.g. Edmondson 1999) were designed for cross-team aggregate comparisons and lack granular multi-dimensional coverage of psychological safety facets for modern remote and cross-functional teams.
decisionLog.methodologicalJustification: Complies with Churchill (1979) requirement to clearly define construct boundaries before developing a de novo measure.
decisionLog.author: Lead Researcher

decisionLog.title: Formal Specification of Reflective Measurement Model
decisionLog.rationalSummary: The three dimensions (Voice Safety, Error Tolerance, Support & Inclusion) are conceptualized as reflective manifestations of a common team interpersonal climate rather than formative ingredients.
decisionLog.methodologicalJustification: Applying factor analysis and Cronbach’s alpha is mathematically justified only under reflective specifications (Bollen & Lennox, 1991; Boateng et al., 2018).
decisionLog.author: Lead Researcher

decisionLog.title: Exclusion of Candidate Item WPSS-13 (Double-Barrelled)
decisionLog.rationalSummary: Item WPSS-13 ("asking questions and requesting promotions") received an I-CVI of 0.50 (well below the 0.78 cutoff for 6 panellists). Reviewers unanimously flagged double-barrelled structure.
decisionLog.methodologicalJustification: Polit & Beck (2006) and Clark & Watson (1995) emphasize that double-barrelled items undermine content validity and confound latent scores.
decisionLog.author: Lead Researcher

decisionLog.title: Rephrasing Item WPSS-01 for Behavioral Specificity
decisionLog.rationalSummary: Cognitive interview subject P1 hesitated over "without fear." Revised to "feel comfortable raising difficult issues and questions during team meetings" to anchor the question in tangible behavioral settings.
decisionLog.methodologicalJustification: Tourangeau, Rips & Rasinski (2000) cognitive model of survey responding indicates clear situational referents improve retrieval accuracy.
decisionLog.author: Lead Researcher

decisionLog.title: Split-Sample Validation Strategy Preregistered
decisionLog.rationalSummary: To avoid capitalization on chance, the recruited pool was formally designated for split-sample cross-validation: N=200 allocated to EFA, and an independent N=220 held out exclusively for CFA.
decisionLog.methodologicalJustification: Clark & Watson (2019) and Hinkin (1998) mandate testing factor structure on an independent sample rather than performing EFA and CFA on the same dataset.
decisionLog.author: Lead Researcher

decisionLog.title: Extraction of 3 Correlated Factors Using Promax Oblique Rotation
decisionLog.rationalSummary: Horn’s Parallel Analysis and Kaiser criterion both supported a 3-factor solution explaining 62.4% of total variance. Oblique Promax rotation was selected given that psychological climate facets are theoretically correlated.
decisionLog.methodologicalJustification: Boateng et al. (2018) recommend oblique rotation over orthogonal Varimax when psychological dimensions are expected to correlate in the population.
decisionLog.author: Lead Researcher

decisionLog.title: Confirmation of 3-Factor First-Order Correlated Model on Independent Sample
decisionLog.rationalSummary: The 3-factor model demonstrated excellent fit on the N=220 validation sample (CFI = .964, TLI = .952, RMSEA = .048 [90% CI: .032 - .063], SRMR = .044). No post-hoc correlated errors were introduced.
decisionLog.methodologicalJustification: Adhering to Hu & Bentler (1999) combinatorial fit criteria without post-hoc cherry-picking preserves confirmatory integrity.
decisionLog.author: Lead Researcher
